description_full: Becton, Dickinson and Company develops, manufactures, and sells medical supplies, devices, laboratory equipment, and diagnostic products for healthcare institutions, physicians, life science researchers, clinical laboratories, pharmaceutical industry, and the general public worldwide. It operates through Medical Essentials, Connected Care, BioPharma Systems, Interventional and Life Sciences segments. It provides peripheral intravenous (IV) and advanced peripheral catheters, central lines, acute dialysis catheters, vascular access technology, vascular care and preparation products, needle-free IV connectors and extensions sets, closed-system drug transfer devices, hazardous drug detections, hypodermic syringes and needles, anesthesia needles and trays, enteral syringes, and sharps disposal systems; IV medication safety and infusion therapy delivery systems, medication compounding workflow system, automated medication dispensing and supply management systems, informatics and analytics and pharmacy automation system, and medication inventory optimization and tracking system; hemodynamic monitoring system; and prefillable drug delivery systems. It also offers specimen and blood collection products; automated blood and tuberculosis culturing, molecular testing, and microorganism identification and drug susceptibility, as well as rapid diagnostic assays, microbiology laboratory automation products, and plated media products; and fluorescence-activated cell sorters and analyzers, antibodies and kits, reagent system, and solution for single-cell gene expression analysis, as well as clinical oncology, immunological, and transplantation diagnostic/monitoring reagents and analyzers. It provides hernia and soft tissue repair, biological and bioresorbable graft, biosurgery, and other surgical products; surgical infection prevention, peripheral intervention, and urology and critical care products. The company was founded in 1897 and is headquartered in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey.
ceo_bio: Mr. Thomas E. Polen Jr. | President, CEO & Chairman | Age 52 | Compensation: $3.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 60K people. Revenue per employee of $364K ranks in the below the sector median among Healthcare peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $44K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (5/10).
financial_summary: Becton, Dickinson and Company is a large-cap healthcare business with a $57.7B market cap on $21.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 47%.

The business throws off $2.7B in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.2×.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 11pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.34x).
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 458 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 33% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.54, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.04 vs 5y 0.45), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $290.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 34% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $238, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $172 to $339 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 41.9 vs 25.5 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-1%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $196 on average, 8% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.79).
It runs a 47% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.04x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.8% of revenue on R&D and 1.2% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.7x net debt to EBITDA ($641.0M of cash against $19.2B of debt), with interest covered 4.2x.
Goodwill makes up 48% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.0% over 3 years, 5.0% over 5 years and 7.8% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -0.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (3.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.2% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 99%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $2.0M sold).
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (1.7% in buybacks and 2.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 43 consecutive years, raising it 3.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 60,000 employees, each generates about $364K of revenue, in line with the Healthcare median, and productivity has risen 7.2% a year.
That works out to $44K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (10x revenue per employee).
